article_title: Effect of Mastery Learning on Senior Secondary School Students' Cognitive Learning Outcome in Quantitative Chemistry
citation: Telimoye Leesi Mitee and Georgina N. Obaitan. (2015). Effect of Mastery Learning on Senior Secondary School Students' Cognitive Learning Outcome in Quantitative Chemistry. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.5. https://www.iiste.org
title: 25-item Chemistry Achievement Test (CAT) on stoichiometry and mole concept
description: The study's outcome instrument is a 25-item chemistry achievement test (CAT) drawn from stoichiometry and mole concept, used to collect data from 401 Senior Secondary 2 chemistry students as pre-test and post-test. It was pilot tested and reliability was established with Kuder Richardson formula 21, yielding "the reliabi lity coefficient (r = 0.7)."
constraints: Content limited to stoichiometry and mole concept topics
target_learning_goals: Quantitative chemistry achievement (stoichiometry and mole concept)
examples: Administered as pre-test to both groups and as post-test after the two-week treatment
key_sources: Telimoye Leesi Mitee and Georgina N. Obaitan. (2015). Effect of Mastery Learning on Senior Secondary School Students' Cognitive Learning Outcome in Quantitative Chemistry. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.5. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1083639

article_title: Students' conceptual knowledge of energy and momentum
citation: Chandralekha Singh and David Rosengrant. (2016). Students’ conceptual knowledge of energy and momentum. https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.07756
title: A research-based 25-item multiple-choice test assessing conceptual knowledge of energy and momentum
description: The article introduces a research-based 25-item multiple-choice test exploring students’ conceptual knowledge of energy and momentum. It covers the work-energy theorem, conservation of mechanical energy, impulse-momentum theorem, and conservation of momentum, and can be administered as a pre-/post-test. The authors state it "can be used to compare the understanding of energy and momentum concepts in courses employing diﬀerent instructional designs and strategies."
requirements: free-response items and think-aloud interviews to ground distractors in common student difficulties
faculty review of performance targets and items for appropriateness and ambiguity
constraints: content deliberately excludes simple harmonic motion, explicit conservative/non-conservative force mention, and center-of-mass reference frames to match most introductory curricula
target_learners: introductory calculus- and algebra-based physics students
target_learning_goals: qualitative understanding of work-energy theorem, conservation of mechanical energy, impulse-momentum theorem, and conservation of momentum
examples: The test was administered as a 50-minute post-test and scored with item difficulty, discrimination, and coefficient alpha.
key_sources: Chandralekha Singh and David Rosengrant. (2016). Students’ conceptual knowledge of energy and momentum. https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.07756

article_title: Student understanding of Symmetry and Gauss' law
citation: Chandralekha Singh. (2016). Student understanding of Symmetry and Gauss' law. https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.07725
title: 25-item multiple-choice test on symmetry and Gauss' law with reliability α = 0.77 and average score about 56%
description: The article presents a conceptual multiple-choice test assessing students' ability to exploit symmetry, predict electric field magnitude and direction using Coulomb's or Gauss' laws, distinguish electric field from electric flux, and identify when Gauss' law easily yields the field and appropriate Gaussian surface shapes. The "final version of the test contains 25 items" administered to 168 students in three introductory calculus-based courses at Pitt, including one honors course. The test was designed with attention to reliability and validity using a test blueprint, and "can be used as a teaching and assessment tool".
requirements: Administered alongside free-response questions and think-aloud interviews to pinpoint student difficulties
constraints: Developed for calculus-based introductory physics courses; design details follow the Energy and Momentum Conceptual Survey approach and will be described elsewhere
target_learners: Students in calculus-based introductory physics courses
target_learning_goals: Distinguishing electric field from electric flux
examples: Administered to 168 students in three courses; average score approximately 56%, reliability coefficient α = 0.77, and 16 questions had point biserial discrimination above 0.4
key_sources: Chandralekha Singh. (2016). Student understanding of Symmetry and Gauss' law. https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.07725
